Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: What Is Data and Why Does It Need Organisation?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: What would you do to find the most popular game among Naresh's and Navya's classmates? (Open-ended process question on data organisation.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the most popular game in their class? (Read and interpret the raw data list to identify hockey as the most frequent.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pari wants to respond to four questions. Put a tick for questions requiring data collection and a cross for those that do not: (a) most popular TV show among classmates; (b) when India got independence; (c) water wasted in her locality; (d) capital of India.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.76
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete the tally-marks frequency table for Shri Nilesh's sweet-preference data. Sub-parts: (a) students who chose jalebi; (b) barfi count; (c) gujiya count; (d) rasgulla count; (e) gulab jamun count.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77
homework.description: Is the frequency table sufficient to distribute each type of sweet to the correct student? Explain. If not, what is the alternative?

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: what kinds of facts or measures qualify as data? Students call out examples; teacher lists them on the board, drawing out that data is any collection of facts, numbers, observations, or descriptions that convey information.

Show a raw unorganised list of students' favourite games (the Naresh and Navya context). Students work in pairs on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.75 (“What would you do to find the most popular game among Naresh’s and Navya’s classmates?”) and Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.75 (“What is the most popular game in their class?”). Pairs share strategies; class settles on counting as the core need.

Introduce tally marks as the organising tool. Together, re-count the games list using tally marks to build a frequency table on the board. Establish the term ‘frequency’ as the count for a category. Students then tackle Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.75 (“Pari wants to respond to four questions—tick if data collection is needed, cross if not”) individually, then share answers.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.76 (“Complete the tally-marks frequency table for Shri Nilesh’s sweet-preference data”) in their notebooks, constructing the full frequency table. A brief whole-class check confirms each sweet’s frequency. Assign Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77 (“Is the frequency table sufficient to distribute sweets to the correct student?”) as take-home work.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse raw data with organised data — watch for those who report the first item in a list as ‘the most popular’ without counting. When tallying, ensure students close every group of five with the diagonal stroke before moving on, or counts will be unreliable. Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.76 on Shri Nilesh’s sweet table is a good self-check: if a student’s tally and frequency columns disagree, they have miscounted.

periods.activity_title: Ordering Data and Reading It With Confidence

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Help Sushri Sandhya figure out from shoe-size data arranged in ascending order: (a) largest shoe size; (b) smallest shoe size; (c) number of students wearing size 5; (d) number wearing sizes larger than 4.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Math Talk: How did arranging the data in ascending order help answer the shoe-size questions?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.78
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write names of trees seen on the way from home to school, record observations, complete a frequency table, then answer: (a) tree found in greatest number; (b) tree in smallest number; (c) any two trees found in equal numbers.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.78
homework.description: Paste a newspaper article, count letters c, e, i, r, x and one other of your choice, fill a frequency table. Sub-parts: (a) most frequent letter; (b) least frequent letter; (c) list the five letters in ascending frequency order and compare with classmates; (d) write the process followed; (e) discuss classmates' processes; (f) what process would you follow with a different article?

time_bands.activity: Present the shoe-size scenario. Students individually apply tally-mark and frequency knowledge to Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.77 (“Help Sushri Sandhya figure out from shoe-size data arranged in ascending order”), answering all four sub-parts.

Class discussion on Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77 (“How did arranging the data in ascending order help answer the shoe-size questions?”). Students articulate that ascending order groups identical values together, making extreme values and counts of a specific size immediately visible. Teacher records key phrases on the board.

Students simulate Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.78 (“Write names of trees seen on the way from home to school, complete a frequency table”) using a class-shared imaginary tree-route scenario the teacher reads aloud (listing 15–18 tree sightings). Each student tallies, forms a frequency table, and answers parts (a)–(c) independently.

Students compare their frequency tables with a neighbour and explain any differences. Teacher assigns Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.78 (“Paste a newspaper article, count letters c, e, i, r, x and one other of your choice, fill a frequency table”) as take-home work.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is counting only the first occurrence of a value in an ordered list and missing repeats — encourage students to scan the entire ordered set before recording a count. Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77 is a genuine reasoning prompt: push students beyond ‘it was easier’ to articulate exactly which question became easier and why. The newspaper-letter task sent home gives authentic data for a future conversation about variability.
materials: A short prepared tree-sighting list to read aloud

periods.activity_title: Symbols, Scales, and the Language of Pictographs

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.2 p.80
textbook_items_in_class.description: Nand Kishor's pictograph on how often middle-school children slept at least 9 hours. Students read the pictograph (each symbol = 10 children) to find: children who always slept ≥9 hours (50), sometimes (25), and never (40). Full solutions provided demonstrating how to handle full and half symbols.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 4.2 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Math Talk: What problems would arise in preparing a pictograph (where one symbol = 10 students, half = 5) if the total number of students in a class is 33 or 27?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.2 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the pictograph of books borrowed from Middle School Ginnori library over a week to answer: (a) day with minimum books borrowed; (b) total books borrowed during the week; (c) day with maximum books borrowed and possible reason.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple pictograph on the board — four rows, each row a category name and a sequence of small identical shapes — without labelling the scale. Students discuss in pairs: what information can they read? What is missing? Class identifies the key structural features needed: a title, category labels, symbols, and a key stating what each symbol represents.

Students open to Example, section 4.2 p.80 (“Nand Kishor’s pictograph on how often middle-school children slept at least 9 hours”). Teacher walks through reading the key (each symbol = 10 children) and interpreting the half-symbol (5 children). Students verify the three answers independently, then the class confirms together.

Students tackle Math Talk, section 4.2 p.83 (“What problems arise if the total is 33 or 27 when one symbol = 10, half = 5?”) in small groups. Groups report: 33 cannot be expressed exactly; 27 requires a non-standard fraction of a symbol. Teacher draws out the key property that a pictograph’s chosen scale must divide all data values cleanly.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.2 p.83 (“Use the pictograph of books borrowed from Ginnori library to answer: day with minimum, total for the week, day with maximum and possible reason”). Answers are shared orally before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently multiply the symbol count by 10 correctly for whole symbols but forget to halve for a partial symbol — highlight the half-symbol in the Nand Kishor example explicitly. The Math Talk on 33 and 27 is where the key insight that scale choice is constrained by the data values first surfaces; this reasoning carries directly into scale selection for bar graphs. For further self-study, Example, section 4.2 p.80 has a complete worked solution worth re-reading at home.

periods.activity_title: Choosing a Scale and Drawing a Pictograph

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.2 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Prepare a pictograph using one symbol = 100 kites for Magan Bhai's kite sales data (Chaman 250, Rani 300, Rukhsana 100, Jasmeet 450, Jetha Lal 250, Poonam Ben 700). Answer: (a) symbols for Rani; (b) maximum buyer; (c) Jasmeet vs Chaman; (d) whether Poonam Ben bought more than double Rani's amount.

time_bands.activity: Brief whole-class review of pictograph structure: title, category labels, symbol, key. Teacher poses: if data values are 250, 300, 100, 450, 250, 700 and one symbol = 100, which values will require half-symbols? Students identify 250 and 450 as needing halves; 700 as requiring 7 full symbols. This surface-level check exposes any residual confusion about scale arithmetic before drawing begins.

Students work through Figure it Out Q2, section 4.2 p.84 (“Prepare a pictograph using one symbol = 100 kites for Magan Bhai’s kite sales data”). They draw the complete pictograph in their notebooks, then answer sub-parts (a)–(d): symbols for Rani, maximum buyer, Jasmeet vs Chaman comparison, and whether Poonam Ben bought more than double Rani’s amount. Teacher circulates and checks that half-symbols are drawn consistently.

Pairs exchange notebooks and peer-check: is the key stated? Are half-symbols used correctly for 250 and 450? Is Poonam Ben’s row the longest? Class discusses part (d): 300 × 2 = 600 < 700, so yes, Poonam Ben bought more than double. Teacher consolidates by summarising when a pictograph works well (values are multiples of the chosen scale) and when it breaks down (values like 33 resist clean symbol-counts).

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error here is drawing 4.5 symbols for Jasmeet (450 ÷ 100 = 4.5) but drawing them at inconsistent sizes or omitting the half-symbol — insist on a visually distinct half. Part (d) is an apply-level check: students must compute 2 × 300 = 600 and compare with 700, not just look at symbol counts. The constraints on pictograph scale identified in the Math Talk (section 4.2 p.83) are the exact source of the half-symbol difficulty here.

periods.activity_title: Bar Graphs: Structure, Scale, and Reading

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.86
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the bar graph of students absent per class (Classes I–VIII) to answer: In Class 2, how many were absent? Which class had maximum absences? Which class had full attendance?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.3 p.87
textbook_items_in_class.description: Horizontal bar graph of vehicular traffic at a busy Delhi road crossing from 6 am to 12 noon (one unit = 100 vehicles). Demonstrates reading maximum (7–8 am, 1200 vehicles), minimum (6–7 am, ~150 vehicles), second highest, and computing combined intervals (8–10 am total ~1800 vehicles).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many total vehicles passed through the Delhi crossing between 6 am and noon?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why do you think so little traffic occurred during 6–7 am compared to later hours?

homework.description: Math Talk on India population bar graph: (a) what questions might you ask friends based on the graph; (b) how much did population increase over 50 years and in each decade?

time_bands.activity: Students examine the Lakhanpal absent-students bar graph in section 4.3. Teacher elicits structural observations: two axes, bars of uniform width, equal spacing, a scale on the vertical axis starting from zero. Students record the three structural rules in their own words.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.86 (“Use the bar graph of students absent per class I–VIII: absences in Class 2, class with maximum absences, class with full attendance”). Reading bar heights against the scale axis is practised here; teacher checks that students align the bar’s top edge with the scale before reading off the value.

Teacher walks through Example, section 4.3 p.87 (“Horizontal bar graph of vehicular traffic at a Delhi road crossing, one unit = 100 vehicles”) using guided questions: which bar is longest? how do we read a bar that ends between grid lines? Students then answer Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.88 (“Total vehicles 6 am to noon”) by summing all bar values, and Figure it Out Q2, section 4.3 p.88 (“Why so little traffic 6–7 am?”).

Students share reasoning for the 6–7 am question; class notes that bar graphs support quick identification of maximum and minimum without recounting. Teacher assigns Figure it Out, section 4.3 p.89 (“Math Talk on India population bar graph”) as take-home work.

periods.teacher_notes: The shift from pictographs (where each symbol carries a count) to bar graphs (where bar length encodes quantity) trips up some students — watch for those reading bar graphs by counting individual units rather than reading the scale directly. For combined intervals in the Delhi traffic example, students must add bar values, not read a single bar; this is where computational errors cluster. Example, section 4.3 p.87 is worth a second read at home for the method of identifying maximum and computing combined totals.

periods.activity_title: From Data Table to Drawn Bar Graph

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.4 p.90
textbook_items_in_class.description: Vertical bar graph of runs scored by Smriti in 8 cricket matches (scores: 80, 50, 10, 100, 90, 0, 90, 50). Demonstrates selecting scale of 1 unit = 10 runs to avoid impractically tall bars and drawing the completed bar graph.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Help Samantha prepare a bar graph for insects seen in a tea garden: Mites 6, Caterpillars 10, Beetles 5, Butterflies 3, Grasshoppers 2.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pooja's partially erased bar graph of railway tickets sold for five MP cities (Vidisha 24, Jabalpur 20, Seoni 16, Indore 28, Sagar 16). Sub-parts: (a) tickets for Vidisha; (b) for Jabalpur; (c) determine the scale; (d) draw correct bar for Sagar; (e) add scale numbers to vertical axis; (f) are Seoni and Indore bars correct?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 4.4 p.98
homework.description: Survey of 120 students' preferred free-time activities (Playing 45, Reading 30, Watching TV 20, Listening to music 10, Painting 15). Draw a bar graph (1 unit = 5 students). Which activity is preferred most after playing?

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the full construction algorithm using Example, section 4.4 p.90 (“Vertical bar graph of Smriti’s runs in 8 cricket matches, scale 1 unit = 10 runs”): draw two perpendicular axes, label the horizontal axis with match numbers, choose scale so the maximum value (100) fits the page, compute each bar height by dividing frequency by the scale unit, draw uniform-width bars with equal spacing. Students narrate each step back.

Students construct the bar graph for Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93 (“Help Samantha prepare a bar graph for insects seen in a tea garden: Mites 6, Caterpillars 10, Beetles 5, Butterflies 3, Grasshoppers 2”) independently in their notebooks. Maximum value is 10; scale of 1 unit = 1 insect is manageable. Teacher checks that axes are labelled and the scale starts at zero.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.93 (“Pooja’s partially erased railway-tickets bar graph: determine scale, fix Sagar’s bar, add axis scale numbers, check Seoni and Indore bars”). This reverses the construction task — students must infer the scale from existing bars. Pairs compare answers before the teacher confirms the correct scale and which bars are wrong. Assign Figure it Out Q9, section 4.4 p.98 (“Draw a bar graph for preferred free-time activities, 1 unit = 5 students”) as take-home work.

periods.teacher_notes: Scale selection is where students most often struggle: they either choose a unit too small (bars overflow the page) or too large (all bars look the same height). The Smriti example is a good anchor — maximum score 100, scale 1 unit = 10 gives exactly 10 units of height, which is manageable. In the Pooja exercise, watch for students who correctly draw Sagar’s bar but forget to add the scale markings to the vertical axis, leaving their graph unreadable. WE-4 (Example, section 4.4 p.91, Imran’s family expenditure) is recommended for self-study on selecting scale for large monetary values.

periods.activity_title: Extended Practice: Constructing and Interrogating Bar Graphs

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.4 p.95
textbook_items_in_class.description: Roll a die 30 times, record outcomes, prepare frequency distribution table with tally marks. Find: (a) number appearing minimum times; (b) number appearing maximum times; (c) numbers appearing equal number of times.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.4 p.95
textbook_items_in_class.description: Faiz's frequency table of Bumrah's wickets in 30 matches. Sub-parts: (a) what information does the table give; (b) possible title; (c) what catches attention; (d) matches with 4 wickets; (e) why Mayank's method of adding 0+1+2+...+7 is wrong; (f) correct method to find total wickets.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 4.4 p.99
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shagufta and Divya's bar graph of tiger counts in India 2006–2022 (in 4-year intervals: 1400, 1700, 2200, 3000, 3700) contains mistakes. Identify and fix the errors in the bars.

time_bands.activity: Students simulate Figure it Out Q4, section 4.4 p.95 (“Roll a die 30 times, record outcomes, prepare frequency table with tally marks; find minimum, maximum, and equal-frequency numbers”) using a teacher-supplied sequence of 30 die outcomes written on the board, so every student works with the same data. Each student builds the tally-frequency table and answers parts (a)–(c).

Students work on Figure it Out Q5, section 4.4 p.95 (“Faiz’s frequency table of Bumrah’s wickets in 30 matches”): interpret the table, write a title, identify what catches attention, find matches with 4 wickets, explain why adding 0+1+2+…+7 gives the wrong total, and compute the correct total. Part (e)—diagnosing Mayank’s error—is discussed briefly as a class: the error conflates the number of wickets with the frequency of that outcome.

Students examine Figure it Out Q11, section 4.4 p.99 (“Shagufta and Divya’s tiger-count bar graph contains mistakes—identify and fix the errors”). Students mark the incorrect bars on the graph and redraw the corrected version. Pairs compare corrections; teacher closes with the rule that bar height must equal frequency divided by the scale unit, and any bar that violates this is wrong regardless of how close it looks.

periods.teacher_notes: Mayank’s error in Figure it Out Q5 (adding the wicket numbers instead of multiplying each by its frequency) is a classic confusion between data value and frequency — it is worth pausing the class to work through the correct computation together. In the tiger-count error-detection task, students sometimes identify only visual oddities (‘the bar looks too short’) without checking against the data; train them to read the scale, compute the expected height, and compare. The die-simulation data shared with the whole class also removes the variability that makes individual-roll tasks hard to check.
materials: Blackboard and chalk (with 30 die outcomes written up)

periods.activity_title: When Design Aids and When It Misleads

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.5 p.103
textbook_items_in_class.description: Would you use vertical or horizontal bars to represent heights of the tallest persons in each class in your school? Why?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.5 p.103
textbook_items_in_class.description: For a table of longest rivers on each continent, would you prefer vertical or horizontal bars? Why? Find the data, make the table and bar graph. Which continents have the longest rivers?

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the principle: bar orientation is a design choice that should mirror the physical reality of the data. Vertical bars are more intuitive when the quantity is height (objects stand up); horizontal bars are more intuitive when the quantity is length or extent (rivers run along the ground). Students state this back in their own words.

Students reason through Figure it Out Q1, section 4.5 p.103 (“Would you use vertical or horizontal bars for heights of the tallest persons in each class? Why?”) in writing. Two or three students share their justifications; class evaluates whether the reasoning invokes the physical-direction principle or merely personal preference.

Teacher introduces infographics: data presentations enriched with imagery. Using the tallest-mountain example from section 4.5, teacher draws two versions on the board — plain vertical bars and triangles of varying widths — and asks: what extra claim does the triangle shape imply? Students identify that varying width implies taller mountains are also wider, which is not in the data and may mislead a reader.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 4.5 p.103 (“For longest rivers on each continent, prefer vertical or horizontal bars? Why? Make the table and bar graph”). They argue for horizontal bars (rivers run horizontally) and sketch a bar graph using approximate data supplied by the teacher. A brief closing discussion: visual appeal is not a reason to distort data — the aesthetic choice must preserve accuracy.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes choose bar orientation for purely aesthetic reasons (‘it looks nicer’) — the lesson’s goal is to develop a principled argument grounded in what the quantity physically represents. The infographic distortion point is subtle: students must see that a design element that carries no data signal (triangle width) nonetheless communicates an unintended claim to a reader; this is the core critical-reading skill of section 4.5. Watch for students who agree that triangles mislead but cannot articulate why — push them to name the implied extra dimension.
materials: Approximate data for longest rivers by continent (teacher-prepared list)

items.prompt: A teacher lists the following hobbies mentioned by 10 students: painting, reading, painting, sports, reading, painting, sports, reading, painting, sports. Which of the following best describes what a frequency table would show for this data?

options.label: A
options.text: A picture symbol for each hobby repeated once per student.

options.label: B
options.text: Each hobby listed once, with a count of how many students mentioned it.

options.label: C
options.text: The hobbies arranged from the longest word to the shortest word.

options.label: D
options.text: The names of the 10 students and their individual hobbies.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Each hobby listed once, with a count of how many students mentioned it. (Painting: 4, Reading: 3, Sports: 3.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A frequency table lists each category once and records the count (frequency) of how many times that category appears in the raw data.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses a raw data list with an organised frequency table; they think a table simply copies names and responses rather than counting them.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student mistakes alphabetical or length-based ordering of category names for frequency organisation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student conflates a frequency table with a pictograph, thinking the table uses picture symbols rather than numerical counts.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to re-read the definition of frequency in section 4.1 before answering again.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the complete frequency table for this data and add a tally column, then state which hobby is most popular.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.75
exercise.description: What would you do to find the most popular game among Naresh's and Navya's classmates? (Open-ended process question on data organisation.)

items.prompt: In a pictograph about books read by students, the key states that one open-book symbol represents 10 books, and a half-symbol represents 5 books. Riya's row shows 3 full symbols and 1 half-symbol. How many books did Riya read?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 35 books. (3 full symbols × 10 = 30, plus 1 half-symbol × 5 = 5; total = 35.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the count of full symbols by the key value, multiply the count of half-symbols by half the key value, and add the two products.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student counted only the 3 full symbols (3 × 10 = 30) and ignored the half-symbol entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student treated the half-symbol as a full symbol (4 × 10 = 40), not applying the halving rule.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have subtracted something from the full-symbol total or miscounted the symbols as 2 full + 1 half.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the key rule for half-symbols in the Nand Kishor example in section 4.2 and work out that example first.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to construct a row for a classmate who read 45 books using the same key, and explain why they need a half-symbol.

exercise.description: Nand Kishor's pictograph on how often middle-school children slept at least 9 hours. Students read the pictograph (each symbol = 10 children) to find: children who always slept ≥9 hours (50), sometimes (25), and never (40). Full solutions provided demonstrating how to handle full and half symbols.

items.prompt: Which of the following is a structural rule that must be followed when drawing a bar graph?

options.label: A
options.text: Each bar must be a different width so the largest category is easiest to see.

options.label: B
options.text: The bars must be arranged in descending order of height.

options.label: C
options.text: The frequency axis must always be placed on the horizontal side.

options.label: D
options.text: The scale on the frequency axis must start from zero.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — The scale on the frequency axis must start from zero. This ensures bar lengths accurately represent the relative sizes of the data values.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the structural rules of bar graphs stated in section 4.3: uniform bar width, equal spacing, and a scale that starts from zero.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student inverts the uniform-width rule, confusing it with a common visual instinct to enlarge the tallest bar.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be thinking of a ranked or ordered list, not the structural requirement of a bar graph.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses vertical and horizontal bar graphs — the frequency axis can be on either side depending on bar orientation.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to look at any two bar graphs in section 4.3 and list three features they both share.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words why starting the scale at a value other than zero would make the graph misleading.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.86
exercise.description: Use the bar graph of students absent per class (Classes I–VIII) to answer: In Class 2, how many were absent? Which class had maximum absences? Which class had full attendance?

items.prompt: A student draws a bar graph to compare the wingspans of five different bird species. She uses triangles instead of rectangles for the bars, making each triangle taller and wider as the wingspan increases. Explain why using triangles of varying widths might mislead a reader of this graph, even if the heights of the triangles are drawn correctly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The varying width of the triangles implies that wider wingspan birds also have a greater physical bulk or body size — a second dimension of information that is not present in the data. A reader glancing at the graph may perceive the largest triangle as representing roughly twice the area (or volume) of the smallest, even when the actual wingspan ratio is smaller. The graph's visual encoding therefore communicates something the data does not support, potentially misleading the reader about relative differences.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the section 4.5 principle that a design element carrying no data signal (here, varying width) nonetheless implies an unintended extra dimension to the reader, distorting the true comparison.

inclusivity.support: Pair the student to discuss aloud what two things change as you move from the smallest triangle to the largest, then write down only the one that reflects wingspan.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if the widths of the triangles were all made equal but the heights still varied, would the graph be accurate? Explain why or why not.

items.prompt: The following shoe sizes were recorded for 12 students and then arranged in ascending order: 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7. Using this ordered data, answer: (a) What is the most common shoe size? (b) How many students wear a size larger than 5? (c) How many more students wear size 4 than size 6?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Size 5 is the most common shoe size — it appears 4 times, more than any other size. (b) 3 students wear a size larger than 5 (two size-6 and one size-7). (c) 3 students wear size 4; 2 students wear size 6; so 1 more student wears size 4 than size 6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count repeated values in the ascending-order sequence to find frequency of each size; compare counts to answer each sub-part.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student underline each size-5 entry in the tick line before counting, then underline sizes 6 and 7 separately for part (b).
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to add one more shoe size (of their choice) to the list so that size 4 and size 5 become equally frequent, and explain what size they would add and why.

items.prompt: A fruit seller recorded the number of mangoes sold across four days: Monday 150, Tuesday 200, Wednesday 50, Thursday 250. She wants to draw a pictograph using one mango symbol to represent 50 mangoes (and a half-symbol to represent 25 mangoes). (a) How many symbols will she draw for Monday? (b) How many symbols will she draw for Thursday? (c) Can she represent Wednesday's sales using only full symbols, with no half-symbol? Justify.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Monday: 150 ÷ 50 = 3 full symbols. (b) Thursday: 250 ÷ 50 = 5 full symbols. (c) Yes — Wednesday's sales are 50, which equals exactly 1 full symbol with no remainder, so no half-symbol is needed. Justification: 50 is a perfect multiple of the scale unit (50), so the division is exact.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each data value by the scale unit (50) to find the number of full symbols; check whether the remainder is zero (no half-symbol needed) or 25 (one half-symbol needed).

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student write each day's value as a multiple of 50 before deciding how many symbols to draw.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if Tuesday's sales were 225 instead of 200, could the seller still use this scale? Explain what difficulty would arise.

items.prompt: A bar graph of daily newspaper sales at a shop shows the following bar heights on a scale where 1 unit = 20 newspapers: Monday 4 units, Tuesday 6 units, Wednesday 3 units, Thursday 7 units, Friday 5 units. (a) On which day were the most newspapers sold, and how many? (b) How many newspapers were sold in total across all five days? (c) How many more newspapers were sold on Thursday than on Wednesday?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Thursday had the most newspapers sold: 7 units × 20 = 140 newspapers. (b) Total = (4 + 6 + 3 + 7 + 5) units × 20 = 25 × 20 = 500 newspapers. (c) Thursday: 140; Wednesday: 3 × 20 = 60; difference = 140 − 60 = 80 more newspapers on Thursday.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each bar's unit height by the scale value (20) to obtain the actual count, then compare or sum as required.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student first write the actual newspaper count next to each bar height before answering any part.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to determine a different scale (other than 1 unit = 20) that would also work for this data and explain why their new scale is valid.

items.prompt: A student records the number of birds spotted in a garden across five mornings: Sparrows 15, Mynas 10, Parrots 5, Pigeons 20, Crows 25. She chooses a scale of 1 unit = 5 birds. (a) What bar height (in units) will she draw for Pigeons? (b) What bar height (in units) will she draw for Sparrows? (c) If she mistakenly draws the Crow bar at 4 units instead of the correct height, by how many birds does her bar undercount?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Pigeons: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 units. (b) Sparrows: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 units. (c) Correct bar for Crows: 25 ÷ 5 = 5 units. She drew 4 units = 4 × 5 = 20 birds. Undercount = 25 − 20 = 5 birds.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each frequency by the scale unit (5) to find the bar height; multiply an incorrect height by the scale unit and subtract from the true frequency to find the undercount.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student complete a small table with columns 'Bird | Frequency | ÷ 5 | Bar height' before answering the question.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to redesign the bar graph using a scale of 1 unit = 10 birds and state which bird counts can no longer be drawn exactly, explaining why.

items.prompt: In an experiment, a student rolled a die and recorded these outcomes across 20 rolls: 1 appeared 3 times, 2 appeared 5 times, 3 appeared 2 times, 4 appeared 4 times, 5 appeared 4 times, 6 appeared 2 times. (a) Which number appeared the maximum number of times? (b) Which numbers appeared an equal number of times? (c) What is the total of all recorded outcomes added together (i.e., 1×3 + 2×5 + 3×2 + 4×4 + 5×4 + 6×2)?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) The number 2 appeared the maximum number of times (5 times). (b) Numbers 4 and 5 both appeared 4 times; numbers 3 and 6 both appeared 2 times — so there are two pairs of equal-frequency numbers. (c) Total = (1×3) + (2×5) + (3×2) + (4×4) + (5×4) + (6×2) = 3 + 10 + 6 + 16 + 20 + 12 = 67.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read frequencies from the frequency table; for part (c) multiply each die-face value by its frequency and sum the products (not merely the frequencies).

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student write each face value and its frequency side by side in a table and circle any rows with the same frequency before answering parts (a) and (b).
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if a seventh roll produced a 3, how would the answers to parts (a) and (b) change? Re-work the affected parts.
